# ABSTRACT
We demonstrate for the first time that the broad-spectrum herbicide glyphosate is a stable transformation product during manganese-driven oxidation of diethylenetriamine penta(methylenephosphonate) (DTPMP), a complexing agent widely  used  in  household  and  industry  applications.  Glyphosate  formation  was observed  at  circumneutral  pH  (i)  in  the  presence  of  MnO2  (with  and  without dissolved O2) as well as (ii) in the presence of Mn 2+  and O2. Maximum glyphosate yields varied with reaction conditions and ranged from 0.06 to 0.16 mol-%. Given the  ubiquitous  presence  of  manganese  in  the  environment  and  wastewater treatment  systems,  Mn-driven  transformation  of  DTPMP  likely  contributes  to glyphosate  formation  under  environmentally  relevant  conditions.  Our  results support recent reports of municipal wastewater as a previously neglected source of  glyphosate  in  European  surface  waters  with  aminopolyphosphonates  as suspected  precursors.  Therefore,  the  current  approach  to  protecting  water resources  from  glyphosate  contamination  needs  to  be  revised,  which  has significant environmental, legal and economic implications.

# INTRODUCTION
The  aminomonophosphonate  glyphosate  is  the  most  widely  used  herbicide worldwide 1 . It is a non-selective herbicide, mostly used to kill weeds that compete with crops. Its utilization has significantly increased following the introduction of genetically modified herbicide-tolerant crops, which allowed for extended glyphosate application periods 1,2 . According to the US National Pesticide Information Center (NPIC) the typical half-life of glyphosate is relatively short (1.5 months) 3  but highly variable in different soils ranging from few days to several years 4-7 .  Environmental  persistence  of  glyphosate  is  reflected  by  its  frequent

detection in ground and surface waters as well as drinking water 8-11 . The major transformation product (TP) of glyphosate in the environment is aminomethylphosphonate (AMPA), which exhibits a longer half-life than glyphosate 7,11,12 .

While glyphosate's toxicity and  cancerogenicity have  been  controversially discussed for decades, glyphosate pollution of water bodies so far has exclusively been  attributed  to  herbicide  applications 13 .  Yet,  two  recent  studies  suggested municipal wastewater as significant additional source for glyphosate in surface waters  in  Europe 14,15 .  Among  the  suspects  are  aminopolyphosphonates  (APPs), which  are  widely  used  in  laundry  detergents  in  the  EU 16 .  They  are  known precursors of AMPA 17-19 , but potentially also of glyphosate 14,20 .

The European Phosphonates Association (EPA) stated a European phosphonate consumption (APPs as well as N-free analogues) of 49,000 tons annually in 2012 16 . A major application area of phosphonates is in detergents and bleach with 7,613 tons used in the detergent sector in Germany in 2019 21 . The three commercially most relevant APPs are aminotris(methylene phosphonate) (ATMP), ethylenediaminetetra(methylene phosphonate) (EDTMP) and diethylenetriamine penta(methylene phosphonate) (DTPMP) 16 .

While the predominant removal process for DTPMP and other polyphosphonates in water treatment plants (WWTPs) is commonly attributed to sorption onto sewage sludge 16,22,23 ,  recent  studies underscore the need to critically examine also the transformation pathways of these compounds 14,15 . In the light of the unexpected findings of widespread glyphosate residues in WWTP effluents 14,15 the consideration of transformation routes of APPs  into potentially  hazardous byproducts is warranted.

While oxidative APP transformation (photolysis, ozonation, Mn 2+ /O2, MnOOH) with AMPA and phosphate as major TPs is well documented in literature 16-19,24 ,  the

evidence for glyphosate formation is limited to ozonation of EDTMP in drinking water 19 , but lacking at environmentally relevant conditions.

Reactants of environmental relevance to consider in this context are manganese oxide  minerals  (MnOx).  They  are  among  the  strongest  naturally  occurring oxidants 25 ,  often  formed  by  microbial  oxidation  of  Mn II ,  leading  to  amorphous structures and high surface areas 25,26 . Manganese minerals occur ubiquitously not only in soils and sediments but are also present in municipal sewage sludge at significant concentrations (600 to 1,500 mg/kg) 27 . Therefore, it is conceivable that manganese oxide minerals or dissolved manganese contribute to the transformation of APPs in municipal wastewater.

The significance of MnOx as well as dissolved Mn 2+  for the oxidation of ATMP and other  APPs  including  DTPMP  has  been  recognised  around  the  turn  of  the millennium  by  Nowack  &  Stone 28-30 .  Recently,  the  transformation  of  IDMP  by manganese dioxide was investigated in detail revealing AMPA and PO4 3-  as main TPs 24 .  High-resolution  mass spectrometry (HRMS) indicated the formation of N -formyl-AMPA (F-AMPA), suggesting oxidation of the terminal carbon of AMPA to form  an  aldehyde  after  C-P  bond  cleavage  of  IDMP.  According  to  the  reaction scheme proposed by Klinger et al. 1997 19 , this would be the intermediate product prior to the formation of the carboxylic acid (in this case involving a methylene moiety).

A prerequisite of glyphosate formation from APPs, however, is the presence of an ethylene moiety on the nitrogen atom whose terminal carbon atom ultimately can be oxidized to a carboxylic acid. Among the high-volume APPs, only EDTMP and DTPMP exhibit this structural feature, the latter one being the quantitatively most significant 31 .

The reaction of manganese oxides with DTPMP or other APPs bearing an ethylene moiety may thus potentially lead to glyphosate formation.

Thus,  manganese  might  be  the  missing  link  for  so  far  overlooked  glyphosate formation from APPs in natural systems and in WWTPs, in line with recent findings calling  for  more  refined  studies  on  APP  transformation 14,15,24 .  Here,  we  present results of systematic laboratory experiments on the formation of glyphosate and AMPA as TPs of DTPMP oxidation by manganese dioxide and dissolved manganese and oxygen. The study was designed to capture relevant environmental conditions regarding pH and the presence or absence of dissolved oxygen.

# RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
We  report  results  of  laboratory  batch  experiments  designed  to  elucidate  the effects of dissolved Mn 2+  and MnO2 mineral concentrations (0.1 g/L vs 1 g/L) and the presence of O2 (atmosphere/21 vol.-% vs N2 atmosphere) on the transformation of 1 mM DTPMP at pH 6.

# DTPMP transformation by MnO2
DTPMP was completely transformed by MnO2 within ≤ 24 h under all conditions studied (see Fig. 2). A control experiment without manganese oxides or dissolved Mn 2+   showed no reactivity (see supplementary Fig. S1). Under oxic conditions, complete DTPMP transformation was observed after 20 min and 24 hours for 1.0 g/L MnO2 and 0.1 g/L MnO2 respectively.

# Formation of TPs from DTPMP
During DTPMP transformation, the formation of various phosphorus-containing TPs was  monitored  using  ion  chromatography  (IC)  coupled  to  inductive-coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Fig. 3 shows an exemplary chromatogram

(1 g/L MnO2, anoxic conditions, reaction time of 2.02 h, aqueous phase) next to a mix-standard of 30 ppb P per compound. As can be seen, multiple P-containing TPs were detected after DTPMP was almost completely transformed ( c (DTPMP) < LOQ). The main TPs identified based on retention times (RT) in all experiments were IDMP and phosphate, in accordance with previous studies 16-18,30 . IDMP was formed  up  to  97 mol-%  (0.1 g/L  MnO2,  anoxic  conditions),  PO4 3-   formed  up  to 153 mol-% (1.0 g/L MnO2, oxic conditions). DTPMP, IDMP and PO4 3-  concentrations over time in the aqueous phase are depicted in supplementary Fig. S2.

In  addition  to  IDMP  and  PO4 3- ,  several  minor  products  were  detected.  The unidentified  TPs  X  and  Z  were  detected  in  all  experiments  at  quantifiable concentrations relative to the initial DTPMP concentration.

In the exemplary chromatogram shown in Fig. 3, a double peak is visible at the RT of  AMPA  (83.0 s),  while  a  triple  peak  is  observed  around  the  RT  of  glyphosate (167.5 s). Both peaks, even if they were considered as the respective compounds, were  below  the  LOQs  (0.9 ppb P  for  AMPA  and  1.7  ppb  P  for  glyphosate)  and therefore represent an almost negligible fraction within the TP spectra. Thus, it is not surprising that the formation of minor products including glyphosate has so far been mostly overlooked.

To verify AMPA and glyphosate formation during DTPMP transformation, we used FMOC derivatization and subsequent quantification by means of reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC) coupled to a triple-quadrupole (QQQ) mass spectrometer, an established trace analysis method for glyphosate and AMPA 34-36 .

# AMPA and glyphosate formation from DTPMP

Glyphosate and AMPA yields were calculated in mol-% based on the analyzed initial DTPMP concentration. The maximum molar yields within the timespans presented below were 0.16 % (1.6 µM) for glyphosate and 10.13 % (95 µM) for AMPA. In analogy to DTPMP transformation, the concentration of oxygen and MnO2 affected the glyphosate and AMPA formation kinetics and stoichiometry.

To  elucidate  the  significance  of  heterogeneous  (MnO2)  and  homogeneous (Mn 2+ /O2) oxidation reactions on product formation, an experiment with 1 mM DTPMP  and  1 mM  dissolved  Mn 2+   (MnCl2)  was  conducted  under  oxic conditions (pH 6, 20 mM MES buffer). Neither glyphosate nor AMPA formation was observed within the first 24 hours. After 123 hours (~5 days), however, 5.4 ± 0.7

mol-% AMPA  and 0.04 ± 0.01 mol-% glyphosate were quantified (see supplementary Fig. S3). Oxygen had a significant effect on glyphosate and AMPA formation kinetics in the MnO2 experiments already in the first 4 hours. Thus, this cannot be traced back to the pure catalytic activity of formed Mn 2+  and oxygen. It is more likely that MnO2 acts as a catalyst supporting the oxidation of formed Mn 2+ by O2 by building a surface complex and stabilizing formed Mn III   33 , which then oxidizes DTPMP and its TPs.

The oxidation of glyphosate and AMPA on manganese oxides has been extensively studied and both compounds can be oxidized by MnOx 12,37-40 . Thus, an additional aspect  necessitating  discourse  evolves  around  the  stability  of  the  formed  TPs glyphosate and AMPA.

To account for longer reaction times, the experiment for the most reactive system (1  g/L  oxic)  has  been  replicated  and  sampled  for  a  longer  timespan  (see supplementary  Fig.  S4).  AMPA  concentrations  increased  until  the  end  of  the experiment and reached a maximum of 206 µM (24 mol-%) after 96 hours (4 days). Glyphosate  was  detected  up  to  a  maximum  of  1.1 µM  (0.1 mol-%),  while  its concentrations fluctuated between 1.1 and 0.6 µM from 1 to 96 hours.

This  experiment  demonstrates  that  AMPA  and  glyphosate  -  even  in  the  most reactive suspension after 4 days - are not completely transformed. Thus, either the  matrix  built  up  in  the  experiment  by  the  abundance  of  other  TPs  inhibits glyphosate  and  AMPA  transformation  and  /  or  glyphosate  and  AMPA  formation exceeds their transformation. Spiking experiments with isotope-labelled glyphosate and AMPA would allow the examination of parallel reactions occurring during the experiment. However, the observation that glyphosate and AMPA in this suspension appear not to be, or are only very slowly, transformed by MnO2 makes these findings even more significant.

# CONCLUSION
Polyphosphonates  as  replacements  of  polyphosphates  and  polycarboxylates  in detergents, laundry products and other applications have so far been regarded as a non-toxic and environmentally acceptable compound class, despite their poor degradability due to the high stability of the C-P bond. However, APPs are known to be less persistent and can be transformed yielding phosphate, IDMP and AMPA by manganese minerals 16,17 , which occur ubiquitously in the environment and also in WWTPs.

Our  study  demonstrates  for  the  first  time  that  manganese  plays  a  key  role  in converting the widely used complexing agent DTPMP in a multi-step reaction to the herbicide glyphosate. The reaction proceeds under environmentally relevant conditions at circumneutral pH value at MnO2 minerals both in the absence and presence of dissolved oxygen but also in homogeneous solution of dissolved Mn 2+ and oxygen. Under all conditions studied, phosphate, IDMP and AMPA were major products but also up to 0.16 mol-% glyphosate were formed. Both the kinetics and yield of DTPMP transformation products were heavily influenced by the reaction conditions (MnO2 and O2 concentration). Once DTPMP was completely removed, the concentrations of AMPA and glyphosate remained stable or even increased within  the  1  to  4  days  periods  of  the  kinetic  experiments.  The  persistence  of glyphosate and AMPA towards the end of the experiment in the presence of excess MnO2 or Mn 2+  is remarkable as both compounds can be oxidized by unreacted MnO2 minerals 12,37,41,42 .

Overall, this study for the first time provides experimental evidence for conversion of a widely  used  non-toxic  commodity  compound  into  a  highly  debated pesticide 1,2,5,43  under environmentally relevant reaction conditions. Thus, it offers a  scientific  basis  to  rationalize  recent  and  unexpected  findings  of  elevated glyphosate concentrations in European WWTP effluents 14,15 .

As a consequence, glyphosate sources for surface water contamination need to be reconsidered  as  well  as  the  significance  of  agricultural  applications  versus wastewater derived sources. Future research should focus on further elucidating effects  of  environmental  conditions  on  glyphosate  formation  from  DTPMP  and related APPs and the identification of key intermediates.

Despite the fact that glyphosate is only a minor TP of DTPMP, yields in the mol-‰ range  nevertheless  may  amount  to  substantial  production  rates  of  glyphosate emitted to surface waters, considering the broad use of DTPMP 16,31,44 .

Thus, the identification of certain high-volume APPs currently used in numerous consumer- and industrial products as precursors of the herbicide glyphosate will have far-reaching scientific, economic and legal implications.

# Design of DTPMP transformation experiments
The  experiments  (duplicates  with  one  control)  have  been  conducted  in  50 mL falcon tubes in the presence of ambient air or in the glovebox ( c (O2) < 10 ppm). For  the  glovebox  experiments,  DTPMP  stock  solution,  MES  buffer  solution  and deionized water have been purged with N2 for one hour under rapid stirring before transfer into the glovebox. Then, DTPMP, MES buffer and water were mixed to yield concentrations of 1 mM DTPMP and 20 mM MES. After taking the timepoint zero aliquot, MnO2 (0.1 or 1 g/L) has been added to start the reaction. For a detailed description of the sampling procedure, we refer to Röhnelt et  al. 24 .  Due  to  the strong sorption of DTPMP to MnO2, the residues were desorbed with 0.1 M NaOH and 0.1 M NaH2PO4 in the ultrasonic bath for 30 minutes instead of 0.1 M NaOH as described in our previous publication. To account for possible parallel homogenous Mn II -catalyzed oxidation by O2 initiated by formed Mn 2+ , an additional experiment with 1mM  MnCl2 (no MnO2) under oxic conditions was conducted. The homogeneous reaction was quenched by addition of cation exchange resin to the aliquot taken from the reaction solution.

Samples were stored in the dark at -20 °C until analysis. Prior to analysis, samples were unfrozen, treated with cation exchange resin (if not done before freezing) and diluted for the respective measurement purpose.

# Quantification of AMPA and glyphosate
AMPA  and glyphosate were quantified using reversed phase (RP) liquid chromatography  (LC)  coupled  to  mass  spectrometry  (MS)  after  derivatization using FMOC  chloride 34-36 . # ABSTRACT
We demonstrate for the first time that the broad-spectrum herbicide glyphosate is a stable transformation product during manganese-driven oxidation of diethylenetriamine penta(methylenephosphonate) (DTPMP), a complexing agent widely  used  in  household  and  industry  applications.  Glyphosate  formation  was observed  at  circumneutral  pH  (i)  in  the  presence  of  MnO2  (with  and  without dissolved O2) as well as (ii) in the presence of Mn 2+  and O2. Maximum glyphosate yields varied with reaction conditions and ranged from 0.06 to 0.16 mol-%. Given the  ubiquitous  presence  of  manganese  in  the  environment  and  wastewater treatment  systems,  Mn-driven  transformation  of  DTPMP  likely  contributes  to glyphosate  formation  under  environmentally  relevant  conditions.  Our  results support recent reports of municipal wastewater as a previously neglected source of  glyphosate  in  European  surface  waters  with  aminopolyphosphonates  as suspected  precursors.  Therefore,  the  current  approach  to  protecting  water resources  from  glyphosate  contamination  needs  to  be  revised,  which  has significant environmental, legal and economic implications.

# INTRODUCTION
The  aminomonophosphonate  glyphosate  is  the  most  widely  used  herbicide worldwide 1 . It is a non-selective herbicide, mostly used to kill weeds that compete with crops. Its utilization has significantly increased following the introduction of genetically modified herbicide-tolerant crops, which allowed for extended glyphosate application periods 1,2 . According to the US National Pesticide Information Center (NPIC) the typical half-life of glyphosate is relatively short (1.5 months) 3  but highly variable in different soils ranging from few days to several years 4-7 .  Environmental  persistence  of  glyphosate  is  reflected  by  its  frequent

detection in ground and surface waters as well as drinking water 8-11 . The major transformation product (TP) of glyphosate in the environment is aminomethylphosphonate (AMPA), which exhibits a longer half-life than glyphosate 7,11,12 .

While glyphosate's toxicity and  cancerogenicity have  been  controversially discussed for decades, glyphosate pollution of water bodies so far has exclusively been  attributed  to  herbicide  applications 13 .  Yet,  two  recent  studies  suggested municipal wastewater as significant additional source for glyphosate in surface waters  in  Europe 14,15 .  Among  the  suspects  are  aminopolyphosphonates  (APPs), which  are  widely  used  in  laundry  detergents  in  the  EU 16 .  They  are  known precursors of AMPA 17-19 , but potentially also of glyphosate 14,20 .

The European Phosphonates Association (EPA) stated a European phosphonate consumption (APPs as well as N-free analogues) of 49,000 tons annually in 2012 16 . A major application area of phosphonates is in detergents and bleach with 7,613 tons used in the detergent sector in Germany in 2019 21 . The three commercially most relevant APPs are aminotris(methylene phosphonate) (ATMP), ethylenediaminetetra(methylene phosphonate) (EDTMP) and diethylenetriamine penta(methylene phosphonate) (DTPMP) 16 .

While the predominant removal process for DTPMP and other polyphosphonates in water treatment plants (WWTPs) is commonly attributed to sorption onto sewage sludge 16,22,23 ,  recent  studies underscore the need to critically examine also the transformation pathways of these compounds 14,15 . In the light of the unexpected findings of widespread glyphosate residues in WWTP effluents 14,15 the consideration of transformation routes of APPs  into potentially  hazardous byproducts is warranted.

While oxidative APP transformation (photolysis, ozonation, Mn 2+ /O2, MnOOH) with AMPA and phosphate as major TPs is well documented in literature 16-19,24 ,  the

evidence for glyphosate formation is limited to ozonation of EDTMP in drinking water 19 , but lacking at environmentally relevant conditions.

Reactants of environmental relevance to consider in this context are manganese oxide  minerals  (MnOx).  They  are  among  the  strongest  naturally  occurring oxidants 25 ,  often  formed  by  microbial  oxidation  of  Mn II ,  leading  to  amorphous structures and high surface areas 25,26 . Manganese minerals occur ubiquitously not only in soils and sediments but are also present in municipal sewage sludge at significant concentrations (600 to 1,500 mg/kg) 27 . Therefore, it is conceivable that manganese oxide minerals or dissolved manganese contribute to the transformation of APPs in municipal wastewater.

The significance of MnOx as well as dissolved Mn 2+  for the oxidation of ATMP and other  APPs  including  DTPMP  has  been  recognised  around  the  turn  of  the millennium  by  Nowack  &  Stone 28-30 .  Recently,  the  transformation  of  IDMP  by manganese dioxide was investigated in detail revealing AMPA and PO4 3-  as main TPs 24 .  High-resolution  mass spectrometry (HRMS) indicated the formation of N -formyl-AMPA (F-AMPA), suggesting oxidation of the terminal carbon of AMPA to form  an  aldehyde  after  C-P  bond  cleavage  of  IDMP.  According  to  the  reaction scheme proposed by Klinger et al. 1997 19 , this would be the intermediate product prior to the formation of the carboxylic acid (in this case involving a methylene moiety).

A prerequisite of glyphosate formation from APPs, however, is the presence of an ethylene moiety on the nitrogen atom whose terminal carbon atom ultimately can be oxidized to a carboxylic acid. Among the high-volume APPs, only EDTMP and DTPMP exhibit this structural feature, the latter one being the quantitatively most significant 31 .

The reaction of manganese oxides with DTPMP or other APPs bearing an ethylene moiety may thus potentially lead to glyphosate formation.

Thus,  manganese  might  be  the  missing  link  for  so  far  overlooked  glyphosate formation from APPs in natural systems and in WWTPs, in line with recent findings calling  for  more  refined  studies  on  APP  transformation 14,15,24 . # RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
We  report  results  of  laboratory  batch  experiments  designed  to  elucidate  the effects of dissolved Mn 2+  and MnO2 mineral concentrations (0.1 g/L vs 1 g/L) and the presence of O2 (atmosphere/21 vol.-% vs N2 atmosphere) on the transformation of 1 mM DTPMP at pH 6.

# DTPMP transformation by MnO2
DTPMP was completely transformed by MnO2 within ≤ 24 h under all conditions studied (see Fig. 2). A control experiment without manganese oxides or dissolved Mn 2+   showed no reactivity (see supplementary Fig. S1). Under oxic conditions, complete DTPMP transformation was observed after 20 min and 24 hours for 1.0 g/L MnO2 and 0.1 g/L MnO2 respectively.

Initial pseudo-0 th order reaction rate constants were  calculated by linear regression  considering  the  time  interval  between  reaction  start  and  complete DTPMP  transformation  (see  Table  1). # Formation of TPs from DTPMP
During DTPMP transformation, the formation of various phosphorus-containing TPs was  monitored  using  ion  chromatography  (IC)  coupled  to  inductive-coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Fig. 3 shows an exemplary chromatogram

As can be seen, multiple P-containing TPs were detected after DTPMP was almost completely transformed ( c (DTPMP) < LOQ). The main TPs identified based on retention times (RT) in all experiments were IDMP and phosphate, in accordance with previous studies 16-18,30 . IDMP was formed  up  to  97 mol-%  (0.1 g/L  MnO2,  anoxic  conditions),  PO4 3-   formed  up  to 153 mol-% (1.0 g/L MnO2, oxic conditions). In  addition  to  IDMP  and  PO4 3- ,  several  minor  products  were  detected.  The unidentified  TPs  X  and  Z  were  detected  in  all  experiments  at  quantifiable concentrations relative to the initial DTPMP concentration.

In the exemplary chromatogram shown in Fig. 3, a double peak is visible at the RT of  AMPA  (83.0 s),  while  a  triple  peak  is  observed  around  the  RT  of  glyphosate (167.5 s). Thus, it is not surprising that the formation of minor products including glyphosate has so far been mostly overlooked.

To verify AMPA and glyphosate formation during DTPMP transformation, we used FMOC derivatization and subsequent quantification by means of reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC) coupled to a triple-quadrupole (QQQ) mass spectrometer, an established trace analysis method for glyphosate and AMPA 34-36 .

Thus, this cannot be traced back to the pure catalytic activity of formed Mn 2+  and oxygen. It is more likely that MnO2 acts as a catalyst supporting the oxidation of formed Mn 2+ by O2 by building a surface complex and stabilizing formed Mn III   33 , which then oxidizes DTPMP and its TPs.

The oxidation of glyphosate and AMPA on manganese oxides has been extensively studied and both compounds can be oxidized by MnOx 12,37-40 . Thus, an additional aspect  necessitating  discourse  evolves  around  the  stability  of  the  formed  TPs glyphosate and AMPA.

Thus, either the  matrix  built  up  in  the  experiment  by  the  abundance  of  other  TPs  inhibits glyphosate  and  AMPA  transformation  and  /  or  glyphosate  and  AMPA  formation exceeds their transformation. Spiking experiments with isotope-labelled glyphosate and AMPA would allow the examination of parallel reactions occurring during the experiment. However, the observation that glyphosate and AMPA in this suspension appear not to be, or are only very slowly, transformed by MnO2 makes these findings even more significant.

# CONCLUSION
Polyphosphonates  as  replacements  of  polyphosphates  and  polycarboxylates  in detergents, laundry products and other applications have so far been regarded as a non-toxic and environmentally acceptable compound class, despite their poor degradability due to the high stability of the C-P bond. However, APPs are known to be less persistent and can be transformed yielding phosphate, IDMP and AMPA by manganese minerals 16,17 , which occur ubiquitously in the environment and also in WWTPs.

Our  study  demonstrates  for  the  first  time  that  manganese  plays  a  key  role  in converting the widely used complexing agent DTPMP in a multi-step reaction to the herbicide glyphosate. The reaction proceeds under environmentally relevant conditions at circumneutral pH value at MnO2 minerals both in the absence and presence of dissolved oxygen but also in homogeneous solution of dissolved Mn 2+ and oxygen. Under all conditions studied, phosphate, IDMP and AMPA were major products but also up to 0.16 mol-% glyphosate were formed. Both the kinetics and yield of DTPMP transformation products were heavily influenced by the reaction conditions (MnO2 and O2 concentration). Once DTPMP was completely removed, the concentrations of AMPA and glyphosate remained stable or even increased within  the  1  to  4  days  periods  of  the  kinetic  experiments.  The  persistence  of glyphosate and AMPA towards the end of the experiment in the presence of excess MnO2 or Mn 2+  is remarkable as both compounds can be oxidized by unreacted MnO2 minerals 12,37,41,42 .

Overall, this study for the first time provides experimental evidence for conversion of a widely  used  non-toxic  commodity  compound  into  a  highly  debated pesticide 1,2,5,43  under environmentally relevant reaction conditions. Thus, it offers a  scientific  basis  to  rationalize  recent  and  unexpected  findings  of  elevated glyphosate concentrations in European WWTP effluents 14,15 .

As a consequence, glyphosate sources for surface water contamination need to be reconsidered  as  well  as  the  significance  of  agricultural  applications  versus wastewater derived sources. Future research should focus on further elucidating effects  of  environmental  conditions  on  glyphosate  formation  from  DTPMP  and related APPs and the identification of key intermediates.

Despite the fact that glyphosate is only a minor TP of DTPMP, yields in the mol-‰ range  nevertheless  may  amount  to  substantial  production  rates  of  glyphosate emitted to surface waters, considering the broad use of DTPMP 16,31,44 .

Thus, the identification of certain high-volume APPs currently used in numerous consumer- and industrial products as precursors of the herbicide glyphosate will have far-reaching scientific, economic and legal implications.

# Design of DTPMP transformation experiments
The  experiments  (duplicates  with  one  control)  have  been  conducted  in  50 mL falcon tubes in the presence of ambient air or in the glovebox ( c (O2) < 10 ppm). For  the  glovebox  experiments,  DTPMP  stock  solution,  MES  buffer  solution  and deionized water have been purged with N2 for one hour under rapid stirring before transfer into the glovebox. Then, DTPMP, MES buffer and water were mixed to yield concentrations of 1 mM DTPMP and 20 mM MES. After taking the timepoint zero aliquot, MnO2 (0.1 or 1 g/L) has been added to start the reaction. For a detailed description of the sampling procedure, we refer to Röhnelt et  al. 24 .  Due  to  the strong sorption of DTPMP to MnO2, the residues were desorbed with 0.1 M NaOH and 0.1 M NaH2PO4 in the ultrasonic bath for 30 minutes instead of 0.1 M NaOH as described in our previous publication. To account for possible parallel homogenous Mn II -catalyzed oxidation by O2 initiated by formed Mn 2+ , an additional experiment with 1mM  MnCl2 (no MnO2) under oxic conditions was conducted. The homogeneous reaction was quenched by addition of cation exchange resin to the aliquot taken from the reaction solution.

Samples were stored in the dark at -20 °C until analysis. Prior to analysis, samples were unfrozen, treated with cation exchange resin (if not done before freezing) and diluted for the respective measurement purpose.

# Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (NMR)
To assure the purity of the acquired DTPMP, a  31 P-{ 1 H}-NMR measurement was conducted (NMR department, Chemistry Department, University of Tübingen).  31 PNMR-spectroscopy  is  a  suitable  analytical  tool  to  characterize  the  purity  of phosphonates, due to the 100% natural abundance of  31 P and the wide range of chemical shift and high sensitivity of the method. 46

10 mg DTPMP and 600 µL of deuterated water (D2O) were mixed and vortexed for 5 s. Afterwards, 600 µL were transferred to an NMR glass tube. The measurement was performed on a Bruker AMX 600 MHz NMR spectrometer (Bruker, Billerica, MA, USA), operating at 242.93 MHz for phosphorous observation with a zgpg30 pulse program. The acquisition parameters used for this experiment with 1D sequence with power-gated decoupling and a 30 ° flip angle were as followed: number of scans:  64,  spectral  width:  96153.844 Hz,  acquisition  time:  0.3407872 seconds. The  spectrum  was  quantitatively  evaluated  using  the  Bruker  Top  Spin  4.1.4

software.

In the  31 P-{ 1 H}-NMR-spectrum (Fig. S 6), two main signals in a ratio of 1:4 can be seen, which represent the phosphonate-group in the middle of DTPMP (δ (ppm): 12.94) and the four phosphonate groups of DTPMP attached to the outer aminemoieties (δ (ppm): 9.23). Impurities are marked with an asterisk. The sum of all signal-integrals is normalized to 100. Impurities of the analysed DTPMP contribute 1.37 %. The purity of the DTPMP used in the experiments is therefore >98.6 %.
